subject: physics
question_text: Define strain energy and derive an expression for it.

mark_split.label: Work as the area under the line

verification.note: Asked in TS March 2019 (Q17) — TS Inter I-Year Physics Paper-I, Section B, 4 marks. The four-way mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: inside the elastic limit F = (YA/L)x, so W = ∫F dx = ½(YA/L)e² = ½ × F × e, and the energy per unit volume u = W/(AL) = ½ × stress × strain.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Strain energy — the definition
lines: A stretching force does work on a wire. Inside
the elastic limit that work is stored in the
wire as potential energy. This stored energy
steps.margin_note: First mark. Two ideas earn it: work is done, and the work is stored as potential energy.
steps.why: The work done is not lost, because inside the elastic limit no permanent set is produced and no energy goes into heat, so all of it is stored.
common_mistakes: Calling strain energy a form of kinetic energy. It is potential energy, stored because the wire is stretched.
Leaving out the words "inside the elastic limit". Past that limit some of the work goes into permanent deformation.

recall.must_convey: That the work done by the stretching force is stored in the wire as potential energy, and that stored energy is the strain energy.
accept: work done is stored as potential energy
strain energy is the energy stored in a stretched wire

steps.memory_tip: Work done in stretching is stored, not lost. The stored energy is the strain energy.

steps.label: The force at extension x
lines: Let a wire of length L and area of cross-
section A be stretched by a force. When the
extension is x, Young’s modulus gives
so the restoring force is proportional to the
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Rearranging Young’s modulus into F = (YA/L)x is the whole of this mark.
steps.why: The force is not constant during the stretch, so it cannot simply be multiplied by the extension. Writing F as a function of x is what makes the work an integral.
common_mistakes: Taking the force as constant and writing W = F × e. The force grows from zero, so the work is half of that.
Writing Y = (F/A)/(L/x) with the strain upside down. Strain is x/L, the extension divided by the original length.

recall.must_convey: That Young’s modulus rearranges to F equals Y A by L times x, so the force is proportional to the extension.
accept: F is Y A by L into x
force is proportional to the extension
reject: the work is stored as potential energy

steps.memory_tip: F = (YA/L)x has the same form as F = kx, so the stiffness of the wire is YA/L.

steps.label: Work done in stretching
lines: The force grows from 0 to F as the extension
grows from 0 to e. Work done in a further
Integrating from x = 0 to x = e,

lines.text: W = ½ (YA/L) e² = ½ × F × e

lines: This is the area of the triangle under the
steps.margin_note: Third mark. The ½ is the mark. It comes from the triangle, because the force grows from zero.
steps.why: A force–extension graph that is a straight line from the origin encloses a triangle, and the area of a triangle carries the factor ½. That is where the ½ in the formula comes from.
common_mistakes: Dropping the ½ and writing W = F e. That would be the area of a rectangle, which needs a constant force.
Integrating F as a constant. F is (YA/L)x and depends on x.

recall.must_convey: That the work is the integral of F dx from 0 to e, which gives half Y A by L into e squared, equal to half F into e, the area of the triangle under the line.
accept: integral of F dx from zero to e
area under the force extension line

steps.memory_tip: Triangle, not rectangle: the force starts at zero, so the work is ½ × F × e.

steps.label: Energy per unit volume
lines: The volume of the wire is A × L, so the strain
energy stored per unit volume is

lines.text: U = ½ F e   ·   u = ½ × stress × strain

steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Split the division as (F/A) and (e/L) so the stress and the strain appear on their own.
steps.why: Dividing by the volume A × L separates neatly into F/A, which is the stress, and e/L, which is the strain, so the same energy is written in a form that holds for any body and not only for this wire.
common_mistakes: Dividing by the length only. The energy per unit VOLUME needs division by A × L.
Writing u = stress × strain and dropping the ½.

recall.must_convey: That dividing by the volume A L gives energy per unit volume u equal to half into stress into strain.
accept: divide by the volume A into L

steps.memory_tip: Divide ½ F e by A × L: F/A is the stress and e/L is the strain.

insider_note: The ½ is the third mark. It comes from the triangle under the line, and it is the line most answers drop.
